newsitem.title: USA: USAir choses Airbus over Boeing in $5 billion deal.
newsitem.headline: USAir choses Airbus over Boeing in $5 billion deal.

text.p: USAir Group Inc. said Wednesday it agreed to buy 120 Airbus Industrie jets and took options on 280 additional planes in a deal worth at least $5 billion.

The order is a major victory for the European constrium and a blow to rival Boeing Co., the world's largest aircraft manufacturer, and McDonnell Douglas Corp., whose commercial aircraft business has struggled.

The deal, which will allow USAir to streamline its fleet and reduce costs, includes firm orders for 120 single-aisle Airbus A319, A320 or A321 jets, with deliveries expected to begin in 1998 at a rate of 30 to 40 a year.
Based on a $45 million published price for the midsized A320 model, the jets would be valued at $5.4 billion, although airlines generally get deep discounts on large orders.
In addition to the firm orders, USAir took options for 120 aircraft with set delivery dates and 160 planes with open-ended dates expected to extend until 2009.
If the Herndon, Va.-based airline exercises all its options and buys 400 jets, the order could be worth $18 billion based on list prices, which would make it among the biggest airplane deals ever.

Boeing, which offered its rival next-generation 737 model in an aggressive competition, was "disappointed" by the loss, said spokeswoman Liz Verdier. But she said the company hopes to sell its wide-body 777 jets to USAir, which also is considering the Airbus A330 model.
Boeing stock fell $1.125 to close at $91.50 on the New York Stock Exchange on a day when the Dow Jones industrial average, of which it is a component, soared 1.6 percent to a record close.

USAir said the twin-engine Airbus jets, which share the same cockpit and engine type, would help it cut costs that are among the highest in the industry, due in part to a mixed fleet that includes McDonnell Douglas DC-9-30s, and MD-80s, Boeing 737-200s and Fokker F-28s.
"The market in the eastern U.S. is moving to a lower-fare environment that brings with it increased demand, USAir Chairman Stephen Wolf said in a statement.
"These aircraft, and the flexibility we have in executing orders among aircraft types, will give us cost-efficient planes of the right size."
The three jet models have from 122 to 168 seats and a maximum range of 2,700 to 3,000 nautical miles.
For Airbus, it was the second major victory this week after the consortium won an order from Emirates airline for 16 A330 jets worth $2 billion, beating an offer of Boeing 767s.
An Airbus spokesman predicted the group would lock up firm orders for 300 planes this year, compared with 106 last year.
"The order backlog is really healthy," said analyst Emmanuel Dubois Pelerin of S&P Adef.
But while airline orders are soaring, both Airbus and Boeing face uncertainty, particularly over their warring plans for new super-jumbo models.
Boeing stock has been under pressure since the disclosure last week that development of a stretched 747 model could cost up to $7 billion.
Airbus, meanwhile, is seeking to change itself into a joint stock company and obtain external financing for a jumbo jet dubbed the A3XX, which would cost $8 billion to design.

USAir said it was in negotiations with manufacturers for engines to power its new Airbus fleet. The airline has a choice of International Aero Engine, a consortium led by Pratt and Whitney and Rolls-Royce Plc; or CFM International, a joint venture of General Electric Co and France's Snecma.
Engines can be worth as much as 25 percent of the value of an airplane.
USAir said it had the flexibility to select among the three models in the A320 family at the time final delivery dates are set.
USAir gained $1.25 to $19.375 on the New York Stock Exchange.
